topicName: Error Handling: block, rescue, always, and ignore_errors
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Error Handling in Ansible: block, rescue, always, and ignore_errors"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, Ansible stops execution on a host as soon as a task fails. While this fail-fast behavior is generally safe, real-world automation often requires graceful error recovery, fallback mechanisms, and mandatory cleanup tasks regardless of success or failure. Ansible provides robust exception handling mechanisms similar to programming languages like Python: block, rescue, always, and ignore_errors."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. Bypassing Failures with ignore_errors"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before diving into blocks, it is important to understand 'ignore_errors'. Sometimes a failing task is non-critical, and you want the playbook to continue regardless of the outcome."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"- name: Attempt an optional cleanup task
  ansible.builtin.command: /usr/bin/old_cleanup_script.sh
  ignore_errors: true"},{"order":6,"type":"heading","text":"2. Grouping Tasks with block and rescue"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you need to handle errors for a sequence of tasks rather than just a single one, use the 'block' keyword. If any task within the 'block' fails, Ansible immediately halts the block execution and jumps to the 'rescue' section."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"- hosts: webservers
  tasks:
    - name: Handle potential deployment failure
      block:
        - name: Stop the application service
          ansible.builtin.service:
            name: app
            state: stopped
        - name: Upgrade application package
          ansible.builtin.yum:
            name: app-package
            state: latest
      rescue:
        - name: Deployment failed, rollback to previous service state
          ansible.builtin.service:
            name: app
            state: started"},{"order":9,"type":"heading","text":"3. Ensuring Cleanup with always"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"The 'always' section runs tasks regardless of whether the 'block' succeeded or failed. This is ideal for cleaning up temporary files, removing firewall rules, or closing database connections."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"- hosts: database
  tasks:
    - name: Perform database migration with safety net
      block:
        - name: Create database snapshot
          ansible.builtin.command: /usr/bin/db_snapshot_create
        - name: Apply schema updates
          ansible.builtin.command: /usr/bin/db_migrate
      rescue:
        - name: Restore from snapshot on failure
          ansible.builtin.command: /usr/bin/db_restore
      always:
        - name: Remove temporary migration tokens
          ansible.builtin.file:
            path: /tmp/migration_token
            state: absent"},{"order":12,"type":"heading","text":"Summary of Best Practices"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use ignore_errors sparingly and only when a failure truly does not impact subsequent tasks."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use block/rescue to encapsulate transactions that need atomic-like rollback behavior."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always use the always section for auditing, logging, or state cleanup tasks."}]
